content:
Stories of Islam's opponents who became Muslims pass quickly from one website to the next, and they grow on the way. A party member becomes the leader of a campaign; a convert's plans acquire a grand mosque. Critics of Islam then point to the inflated details and dismiss the whole story.

Some of these stories are true and well documented, and one popular version is false in its details. The difference matters, because a Muslim who repeats an embellished story hands the critic an easy win.

This article aims to provide context to those stories, insha'Allah, in four cases checked against the record: three men whose opposition and later conversion are documented, and one whose story was embellished. The Quran sets the rule for the checking: "If a wicked person comes to you with any news, ascertain the truth, lest ye harm people unwittingly" (49:6).[1]

Joram van Klaveren sat in the Dutch parliament for Geert Wilders' Party for Freedom (PVV) from 2010 to 2014, and was known for his attacks on Islam. After leaving politics he began writing a book against Islam. In February 2019 he announced that he had become a Muslim.[2]

He described the change on Dutch radio: "During that writing I came across more and more things that made my view on Islam falter."[2] The book he finished, Apostate: From Christianity to Islam in Times of Secularisation and Terror, told the story of his conversion in place of the case he had set out to make.[3]

His record on both sides is public, and nothing in it needs embellishment.

Arnoud van Doorn was a member of the same party, and he helped distribute Fitna, the anti-Islam film made by Wilders. The party broke with him in December 2011, and he announced his conversion to Islam in April 2012, then performed the hajj.[4]

He said that the reaction of Muslims around the world to Fitna made him want to learn more about Islam, and that he regretted his part in the film.[4] Euronews, reporting van Klaveren's conversion in 2019, noted that van Doorn had made the same change before him.[2]

The two men left the same party by different roads. Their conversions are two stories, and neither is evidence of a movement.

Richard "Mac" McKinney, a former United States Marine, went to the Islamic Center of Muncie, Indiana, one Friday afternoon in 2009 meaning to plant a bomb there. The film made about him calls him a Marine "suffering from PTSD and filled with hatred who planned to blow up the mosque in his small Indiana town."[5]

The congregation met him with kindness. Bibi Bahrami, a co-founder of the center, invited him to her home for an Afghan dinner, and CNN's John Blake reports that she "played a pivotal role in McKinney's conversion": "Eight months after McKinney's initial visit to the mosque, he converted to Islam. After the ceremony he was greeted with what he called 'a mosh pit of hugs' from the people he once intended to harm." He later served two years as the center's president.[6]

His story is told in Stranger at the Gate, Joshua Seftel's documentary short, which was nominated for the Academy Award in 2023.[5] It is the Quran's instruction acted out: "Repel (Evil) with what is better: Then will he between whom and thee was hatred become as it were thy friend and intimate!" (41:34).[1]

Daniel Streich, a Swiss local politician, was a long-time member of the Swiss People's Party (SVP), the party that backed the 2009 referendum banning new minarets. Swiss voters accepted the ban by 57.5%.[7] Versions of his story spread online in early 2010 claiming that he had led the campaign against minarets and was now building a beautiful mosque.[8]

Jason Hamza van Boom traced the claims back to the Swiss reports. Streich had converted two years earlier and resigned from the party when its campaign became too much for him. Van Boom called the story that he led the campaign "a complete fabrication", and found "no evidence that he's planning to build any mosque, beautiful or not."[8]

Streich's real story is worth telling: a party member who became a Muslim and left over the campaign. The inflated version only damages it.

The bottom line

Three documented cases show men who opposed Islam and later embraced it: van Klaveren while writing a book against it, van Doorn after distributing Fitna, and McKinney after coming to a mosque to bomb it. The fourth, Streich, is a true conversion carried online with invented details.

A Muslim who shares such stories owes them the Quran's standard: check the news, and keep to justice even towards those who once opposed us, "and let not the hatred of others to you make you swerve to wrong and depart from justice" (5:8).[1] The accurate version is always the stronger one. Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Quran 5:8; 41:34; 49:6, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  2. Pascale Davies, "Dutch former far-right politician converts to Islam", Euronews, 5 February 2019.
  3. Joram van Klaveren, Apostate: From Christianity to Islam in Times of Secularisation and Terror, as listed in the English Wikipedia article "Joram van Klaveren".
  4. "Arnoud van Doorn", English Wikipedia, on his part in distributing Fitna, his conversion announced in April 2012 and his hajj.
  5. "Stranger at the Gate" and "FAQs", strangeratthegate.com, the film's official site.
  6. John Blake, "US Marine Richard 'Mac' McKinney went to Islamic center in Muncie, Indiana to plant bomb, but intended victims saved his life", CNN, read in the text republished by ABC7 Chicago, 8 October 2022; CNN's own page (edition.cnn.com, 8 March 2023) refused automated reading.
  7. Abdelhafidh Abdeleli, "Switzerland's controversial minaret ban, ten years on", SWI swissinfo.ch, 29 November 2019.
  8. Jason Van Boom, "A Swiss Politician's Conversion: Facts vs Myth", OpEdNews, 10 February 2010, first published at Tikkun Daily, 4 December 2009.
